newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court questions suicide right.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court questions suicide right.

text.p: Taking up an issue of historic import to American society, the Supreme Court on Wednesday appeared deeply sceptical about proposals to create a constitutional right for the terminally ill to get medical help in committing suicide.

While the high court did not take a firm position during arguments on the right-to-die controversy, several justices expressed reservations about overturning existing state bans on doctor-assisted suicide.

As sign-carrying demonstrators on both sides of the dispute marched outside the building in clear, cold weather, the court grappled with whether to give constitutional protection to a bitterly controversail practice never previously allowed.
Lawyers arguing in favour of a new right said mentally competent, terminally ill patients should be allowed to ask their doctor for help in ending their lives to relieve needless pain and suffering.
But government lawyers replied that medical groups oppose doctor-assisted suicide, said it has never been allowed in the nation's history and warned it could lead to dangerous abuse.

"It would be a grave mistake for the court to impose on 50 states what has never been tried in a single state," said Acting U.S. Solicitor General Walter Dellinger, the federal government's top courtroom lawyer, in reflecting President Bill Clinton's repeated opposition to doctor-assisted suicide.
Dellinger suggested legalising assisted suicide might create dangerous economic temptations, saying, "The least costly treatment for any illness is lethal medication."

Kathryn Tucker, representing physicians challenging the Washington state ban, said a patient should have a right to make their own decision about "bodily integrity," free from government interference.
But Justice Sandra Day O'Connor expressed concern about the argument, commenting, "It would result in a flow of cases through the court system for heaven knows how long."
Justice Anthony Kennedy said state legislatures, which reflect the views of the people, may be the proper place to decide the moral and other issues surrounding assisted suicide.
"You are asking us, in effect, to declare unconstitutional the laws in 50 states," Kennedy said to the rights proponents.

Justice David Souter said more experience around the world may be needed before an informed judgment can be reached on the issue, and added that for the court to make it legal now "would just be guess-work."

William Williams, representing the state of Washington -- scene of one of two cases that brought this issue before the court -- said assisted suicide has only been allowed in the Netherlands and Australia's Northern Territory. He said Canada and Britain recently rejected the idea.

The case did not involve Dr. Jack Kevorkian, a retired pathologist in Michigan and America's best-known advocate and practitioner of medically assisted suicide, who has publicly acknowledged attending more than 40 deaths since 1990.
He has never been convicted, although he has been charged, and come to symbolise the whole controversy to many Americans.

Justice John Paul Stevens may have been referring to Kevorkian when he said he was unaware of any doctor ever being convicted for helping a patient commit suicide. He seemed to be suggesting those supporting assisted suicide were pursuing that course without need of formal legalisation.
